Five 3d orbitals
All five 3d orbitals are shown. Click an orbital or its label to focus it; drag to rotate the true 3D surfaces.

plan.contextChunk: This figure shows the three-dimensional probability-density surfaces of all five 3d orbitals, presented as a row of five separate diagrams each drawn on labeled x, y, and z coordinate axes. The first three orbitals — 3d_xy, 3d_xz, and 3d_yz — each display four lobes of electron density directed between the pairs of Cartesian axes indicated by their subscripts, with transparent colored planes highlighting the nodal planes through which the wavefunction passes through zero; for example, the 3d_xy orbital has lobes oriented diagonally between the x and y axes in the xy-plane pointing upwards. The fourth orbital, 3d_z², has a distinct shape with two primary lobes extending along the z-axis and a torus-shaped ring of electron density encircling the nucleus in the xy-plane, making it unlike the other four. The fifth orbital, 3d_x²−y², has four lobes directed along the x and y axes themselves rather than between them, distinguishing it from the 3d_xy orbital despite both lying predominantly in the xy-plane. This figure establishes the spatial orientations and unique geometries of the five degenerate 3d orbitals, which are essential for understanding directional bonding, crystal field splitting, and the distinctive chemistry of transition-metal compounds.

elements: five side-by-side orbital diagrams arranged in a horizontal row
for each orbital diagram: black x-axis with arrowhead and italic label x
for each orbital diagram: black y-axis with arrowhead and italic label y
for each orbital diagram: black vertical z-axis with arrowhead and italic label z
central nucleus/origin marker at the intersection of the three axes for each diagram
bottom label under first diagram: 3d_xy
bottom label under second diagram: 3d_xz
bottom label under third diagram: 3d_yz
bottom label under fourth diagram: 3d_z^2
bottom label under fifth diagram: 3d_x^2-y^2
3d_xy orbital: four rounded lobes in the xy plane, directed between the x and y axes
3d_xy orbital nodal plane x=0, the yz plane, drawn as a translucent vertical green plane
3d_xy orbital nodal plane y=0, the xz plane, drawn as a translucent vertical pink plane
3d_xz orbital: four rounded lobes in the xz plane, directed between the x and z axes
3d_xz orbital nodal plane y=0, the xz-related vertical plane shown as a translucent pink plane in the source-style view
3d_xz orbital nodal plane z=0, the xy plane, drawn as a translucent horizontal cyan plane
3d_yz orbital: four rounded lobes in the yz plane, directed between the y and z axes
3d_yz orbital nodal plane x=0, the yz-related vertical green plane
3d_yz orbital nodal plane z=0, the xy plane, drawn as a translucent horizontal cyan plane
3d_z^2 orbital: two large rounded lobes aligned along the z-axis, one above and one below the origin
3d_z^2 orbital: torus-shaped donut ring of electron density around the origin in the xy plane
3d_z^2 orbital nodal surfaces: two translucent double-cone surfaces above and below the xy plane, shown only when selected
3d_x^2-y^2 orbital: four rounded lobes lying in the xy plane and pointing directly along the positive x, negative x, positive y, and negative y axes
3d_x^2-y^2 orbital nodal planes: two vertical diagonal planes x=y and x=-y, shown only when selected

interactions.teaches: Clicking an orbital label focuses attention on one 3d orbital at a time, making its lobe orientation and nodal planes easier to compare against the dimmed set of the other four orbitals
Rotating the selected orbital reveals that the lobes and nodal planes are genuinely three-dimensional surfaces, not flat drawings

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use five local coordinate frames spaced horizontally about 3.2 world units apart, centered at x = -6.4, -3.2, 0, 3.2, and 6.4. Each local axis should be about 1.35 units long with arrowheads. Orbital lobes should fit in a local cube of roughly ±0.9 units before selection; selected orbital can scale to about 1.6× and visually move slightly forward/up or remain centered while others dim to 15–25% opacity. Dominant colors: axes black #000000; orbital lobes yellow-to-orange with warm highlights, approximately #ffe36a, #ffb23a, and orange rim #ff7f1f; nodal planes translucent pink #e78bdc at alpha 0.25, green #93e89a at alpha 0.25, and cyan #9be7ed at alpha 0.25. Approximate analytic orbital forms for orientation: d_xy proportional to xy, d_xz proportional to xz, d_yz proportional to yz, d_z2 proportional to 2z^2 - x^2 - y^2, and d_x2-y2 proportional to x^2 - y^2. For d_xy, d_xz, and d_yz, render four ellipsoidal lobes oriented in the corresponding coordinate plane between the named axes. For d_z2, render two elongated ellipsoids along z plus a torus in the xy plane. For d_x2-y2, render four ellipsoids directed along ±x and ±y. Nodal planes: d_xy has x=0 and y=0; d_xz has x=0 and z=0; d_yz has y=0 and z=0; d_x2-y2 has x=y and x=-y. d_z2 has conical nodal surfaces rather than planes; show these as translucent cones when selected and label them as nodal surfaces.
interactionPlan.notes: Use a standard isometric/axonometric camera with orthographic projection to match the source figure’s non-converging textbook style. Build each orbital as a reusable group containing axes, label, lobes, and optional nodal surfaces. Labels should be clickable text sprites or mesh text. On click, set the selected group to full opacity and enlarged scale, dim all other orbital groups, and increase opacity/saturation of that orbital’s nodal surfaces. In the default unselected view, show the three source-visible nodal plane sets for d_xy, d_xz, and d_yz, while keeping d_z2 cones and d_x2-y2 diagonal planes hidden until selected to avoid clutter.

authoredContext: This figure includes diagrams of five d orbitals. Each diagram includes three axes. The z-axis is vertical and is denoted with an upward pointing arrow. It is labeled “z” in the first diagram. Arrows similarly identify the x-axis with an arrow pointing from the rear left to the right front, diagonally across the figure and the y-axis with an arrow pointing from the left front diagonally across the figure to the right rear of the diagram. These axes are similarly labeled as “x” and “y.” The first through third diagrams show four orange balloon-like shapes. These diagrams differ however in the orientation of the shapes along the axes and the x-, y-, and z-axis labels have each been replaced with the letter L. Planes are added to the figures to help show the orientation differences with these diagrams. In the first diagram, a green plane is oriented vertically through the length of the x-axis and a blue plane is oriented horizontally through the length of the y-axis. The balloon shapes extend from the origin to the spaces between the positive z- and negative y- axes, positive z- and positive y- axes, negative z- and negative y- axes, and negative z- and positive y- axes. This diagram is labeled, “3 d subscript ( y z ).” In the second diagram, a green plane is oriented vertically through the x- and y- axes and a blue plane is oriented horizontally through the length of the x-axis. The balloon shapes extend from the origin to the spaces between the positive z- and negative x- axes, positive z- and positive x- axes, negative z- and negative x- axes, and negative z- and positive x- axes. This diagram is labeled “3 d subscript ( x z ).” In the third diagram, a pink plane is oriented vertically through the length of the y-axis and a green plane is oriented vertically through the length of the x-axis. The balloon shapes extend from the origin to the spaces between the positive x- and negative y- axes, positive x- and positive y- axes, negative x- and negative y- axes, and negative x- and positive y- axes. This diagram is labeled, “3 d subscript ( x y ).” The fourth diagram has a pair of the orange balloon-like shapes are present and extend from the origin above and below along the vertical axis. An orange toroidal or donut shape is positioned around the origin, oriented through the x- and y- axes. This shape extends out to about a third of the length of the positive and negative regions of the x- and y- axes. This diagram is labeled, “3 d subscript ( z superscript 2 ).” In the fifth diagram, four orange balloon-like shapes extend from a point at the origin out along the x- and y- axes in positive and negative directions covering just over half the length of the positive and negative x- and y- axes. Beneath the diagram is the label, “3 d subscript ( x superscript 2 minus y superscript 2 ).”

3d orbitals
Click a label or orbital to focus it. Drag the scene to rotate.

discrepancies: The five orbitals are arranged on a diagonal receding line instead of the source's straight horizontal row with equal visual scale.
All orbital lobes are rendered mostly orange/yellow, whereas the source uses more distinct warm red/orange/yellow/green phase-like coloring across lobes.
The 3d_x2−y2 orbital appears as a flat four-petal clover from the default view, not like the source's two prominent opposing vertical lobe pairs with the other pair mostly hidden by projection.
The 3d_z2 torus and polar lobes are smaller/thinner than in the source, making the characteristic donut-and-dumbbell form less dominant.
The nodal/coordinate planes for 3d_xz and 3d_yz appear to include the lobe plane rather than matching the source's shown coordinate-plane orientations.
The labels are present but the bottom orbital labels and axis labels are smaller and less textbook-like than the large italic labels in the source.
evaluation.notes: The figure is recognizable as the five 3d orbitals and has useful focus interactions, but the layout, colors, default viewing angle, and some plane/orbital proportions diverge noticeably from the source.
action_items: Arrange the five orbitals in a straight horizontal row with consistent size and the same apparent viewpoint as the source.
Use stronger source-like lobe coloring, including distinct red/orange/yellow/green phase shading rather than nearly uniform orange lobes.
Adjust the 3d_z2 torus and polar lobes to be fuller and more visually dominant.
Change the default view/proportions of 3d_x2−y2 so it matches the source's two prominent opposing lobe pairs rather than a flat clover.
plan_action_items: Recheck the intended coordinate/nodal planes for 3d_xz and 3d_yz and specify the source-matching plane orientations explicitly.

feedback.rationale: The figure concept is recognizable and interactivity works, while the main problems are implementation-level layout, camera, color, scale, proportions, and plane-orientation refinements rather than a fundamentally wrong plan.

discrepancies: The entire row of orbitals is rendered much too small with excessive whitespace, whereas the source figure fills the width with large individual orbital drawings.
The lobes are generally too small, separated, and petal-like; the source lobes are larger, more bulbous, and overlap visually around the nucleus.
The orbital coloring is less faithful: the source uses stronger warm phase-like red/orange/yellow variation, while the generated lobes are mostly uniform orange/yellow gradients.
The translucent nodal planes in the first three orbitals are present but smaller and fainter than the prominent colored planes in the source.
Extra in-scene annotations such as 'nodal surfaces' and 'nodal planes' appear in the generated view but are not present in the source figure.
The 3d_z² and 3d_x²−y² shapes are recognizable but their proportions and silhouette do not closely match the source, especially the torus-to-lobe balance and the apparent width of the x²−y² lobes.
evaluation.notes: The five orbitals, axes, labels, and nodal planes are conceptually recognizable, but the rendering is far too small and the lobe proportions/colors are only moderately faithful to the textbook figure.
action_items: Increase the default scale or camera zoom so the five orbitals occupy the width of the canvas similarly to the source.
Enlarge and reshape the lobes to be more bulbous and overlapping, especially for 3d_xy, 3d_z², and 3d_x²−y².
Match the source's stronger warm color variation and make the visible nodal planes larger and more prominent.
Hide extra nodal-surface/nodal-plane annotations in the default all-orbitals view so the initial composition matches the source more closely.

The first three orbitals — 3d_xy, 3d_xz, and 3d_yz — each display four lobes of electron density directed between the pairs of Cartesian axes indicated by their subscripts, with transparent colored planes highlighting the nodal planes through which the wavefunction passes through zero; for example, the 3d_xy orbital has lobes oriented diagonally between the x and y axes in the xy-plane pointing upwards. The fourth orbital, 3d_z², has a distinct shape with two primary lobes extending along the z-axis and a torus-shaped ring of electron density encircling the nucleus in the xy-plane, making it unlike the other four. The fifth orbital, 3d_x²−y², has four lobes directed along the x and y axes themselves rather than between them, distinguishing it from the 3d_xy orbital despite both lying predominantly in the xy-plane. This figure establishes the spatial orientations and unique geometries of the five degenerate 3d orbitals, which are essential for understanding directional bonding, crystal field splitting, and the distinctive chemistry of transition-metal compounds.

elements: five side-by-side orbital diagrams arranged in a horizontal row
for each orbital diagram: black x-axis with arrowhead and italic label x
for each orbital diagram: black y-axis with arrowhead and italic label y
for each orbital diagram: black vertical z-axis with arrowhead and italic label z
central nucleus/origin marker at the intersection of the three axes for each diagram
bottom label under first diagram: 3d_xy
bottom label under second diagram: 3d_xz
bottom label under third diagram: 3d_yz
bottom label under fourth diagram: 3d_z^2
bottom label under fifth diagram: 3d_x^2-y^2
3d_xy orbital: four rounded lobes in the xy plane, directed between the x and y axes
3d_xy orbital nodal plane x=0, the yz plane, drawn as a translucent vertical green plane
3d_xy orbital nodal plane y=0, the xz plane, drawn as a translucent vertical pink plane
3d_xz orbital: four rounded lobes in the xz plane, directed between the x and z axes
3d_xz orbital nodal plane y=0, the xz-related vertical plane shown as a translucent pink plane in the source-style view
3d_xz orbital nodal plane z=0, the xy plane, drawn as a translucent horizontal cyan plane
3d_yz orbital: four rounded lobes in the yz plane, directed between the y and z axes
3d_yz orbital nodal plane x=0, the yz-related vertical green plane
3d_yz orbital nodal plane z=0, the xy plane, drawn as a translucent horizontal cyan plane
3d_z^2 orbital: two large rounded lobes aligned along the z-axis, one above and one below the origin
3d_z^2 orbital: torus-shaped donut ring of electron density around the origin in the xy plane
3d_z^2 orbital nodal surfaces: two translucent double-cone surfaces above and below the xy plane, shown only when selected
3d_x^2-y^2 orbital: four rounded lobes lying in the xy plane and pointing directly along the positive x, negative x, positive y, and negative y axes
3d_x^2-y^2 orbital nodal planes: two vertical diagonal planes x=y and x=-y, shown only when selected

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use five local coordinate frames spaced horizontally about 3.2 world units apart, centered at x = -6.4, -3.2, 0, 3.2, and 6.4. Each local axis should be about 1.35 units long with arrowheads. Orbital lobes should fit in a local cube of roughly ±0.9 units before selection; selected orbital can scale to about 1.6× and visually move slightly forward/up or remain centered while others dim to 15–25% opacity. Dominant colors: axes black #000000; orbital lobes yellow-to-orange with warm highlights, approximately #ffe36a, #ffb23a, and orange rim #ff7f1f; nodal planes translucent pink #e78bdc at alpha 0.25, green #93e89a at alpha 0.25, and cyan #9be7ed at alpha 0.25. Approximate analytic orbital forms for orientation: d_xy proportional to xy, d_xz proportional to xz, d_yz proportional to yz, d_z2 proportional to 2z^2 - x^2 - y^2, and d_x2-y2 proportional to x^2 - y^2. For d_xy, d_xz, and d_yz, render four ellipsoidal lobes oriented in the corresponding coordinate plane between the named axes. For d_z2, render two elongated ellipsoids along z plus a torus in the xy plane. For d_x2-y2, render four ellipsoids directed along ±x and ±y. Nodal planes: d_xy has x=0 and y=0; d_xz has x=0 and z=0; d_yz has y=0 and z=0; d_x2-y2 has x=y and x=-y. d_z2 has conical nodal surfaces rather than planes; show these as translucent cones when selected and label them as nodal surfaces.
interactionPlan.notes: Use a standard isometric/axonometric camera with orthographic projection to match the source figure’s non-converging textbook style. Build each orbital as a reusable group containing axes, label, lobes, and optional nodal surfaces. Labels should be clickable text sprites or mesh text. On click, set the selected group to full opacity and enlarged scale, dim all other orbital groups, and increase opacity/saturation of that orbital’s nodal surfaces. In the default unselected view, show the three source-visible nodal plane sets for d_xy, d_xz, and d_yz, while keeping d_z2 cones and d_x2-y2 diagonal planes hidden until selected to avoid clutter.

discrepancies: The five orbitals are rendered very small in the middle of a large blank canvas instead of filling the horizontal composition like the source figure.
All orbital lobes use nearly the same orange/yellow glossy coloring, while the source shows distinct multicolored lobes suggesting different phases and stronger visual separation.
